description.narrative:
Projektet "Towards Generative Resilience and Climate Adaptation for displacement affected communities in Somalia" (TERRA) implementeras av konsortiet Building Resilient Communities in Somalia (BRCiS), lett av Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC).
Projektet bygger på tidigare BRCiS-projekt, där detta projekt adderar en ny innovativ typ av resiliensaktiviteter som direkt kopplar samman landsbygdssamhällen med hushåll som flytt till stadsområden, för förbättrad livsmedelssäkerhet och ökad tillgång till marknader. Somaliska flyktingkvinnor i stadsområden har starka ekonomiska kopplingar med jordbrukare på landsbygden i de områden de flytt från, vilket är avgörande för livsmedelshandel i urbana marknader. Många fördrivna hushåll fortsätter också att odla på landsbygden, och aktiviteter för att återställa ekosystem kommer att öka deras produktivitet. Genom att arbeta tillsammans mellan landsbygds­ och stadssamhällen kan båda grupper ytterligare stärka sin motståndskraft mot chocker och öka sin produktion, försörjning och inkomst.
Detta tillvägagångssätt att medvetet programmera mellan landsbygd och städer är nytt i Somalia, där projekt traditionellt riktar sig antingen mot landsbygdsområden, eller stadsområden genom hållbara lösningar. BRCiS förutser att detta nya tillvägagångssätt kommer fungera som bevis på stärkt motståndskraft för inkluderade grupper och blir en modell för kunskapsspridning av nya metoder.

The project "Towards Generative Resilience and Climate adaptation for displacement affected communities in Somalia" (TERRA) is implemented by the Building Resilient Communities in Somalia (BRCiS) consortium, led by Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC).
The project builds on the third phase of the larger BRCiS consortium support, where this intervention would add a new innovative type of resilience activities that directly connect rural communities with displaced populations in urban areas for improved food security and increase access to markets.
Studies show that displaced women in urban areas of Somalia maintain strong economic connections with rural farmers in their areas of origin, which is vital for agricultural trade in urban markets. Many displaced households also continue to farm in rural areas, and ecosystem restoration efforts will sustain and increase their food productivity. By working together between rural and urban communities, both groups can further strengthen their resilience to shocks and increase their livelihood sustainability and income.
This approach to deliberately program along the rural-­urban continuum is new to Somalia, where resilience programs traditionally target either rural areas, or urban areas though durable solutions activities. Over time, BRCiS anticipates that this new approach will empower the target communities to serve as proof of strengthened resilience and exemplify models for further replication.

The overall program goal of the project is to improve the food security of displaced populations in Somalia, including both urban/peri-urban communities hosting internally-displaces persons and the rural communities from which populations are displaced, among other cases, by climate shocks and environment degradation.
The expected outputs of the contribution are:
Output 1 Displaced populations increase their knowledge and use of regenerative, context-specific food production and environmental management practices.
Output 2 - Rural and urban displaced population actors along local food value chains work together to create value and augment their climate adaptation capacities.
Output 3 - Target communities benefit from and contribute to functioning Early Warning Systems linked to Early Action response mechanisms.
Target group and geographic locations
The project primarily targets vulnerable displacement-affected communities in both urban and rural areas and will reach 165 046 individuals.
TERRA will be implemented in 20 rural communities and 13 urban settlements split into four clusters across Bardere, Baidoa, Galkcayo and Jariban Districts. These four clusters and rural communities are based on BRCiS III's nature based area delineation exercise that produced clusters based on participatory mapping exercise of communities' natural resources, how they are being used and by whom and with what implication for conflict and stability. The 13 urban settlements have been provisionally selected based on their high level of socio-economic vulnerability and their pre-existing linkages to their surrounding rural areas.

description.narrative:
Some results of the first implementation year:
- 400 stakeholders (government extension workers, community committee members, and IDP representatives) were trained in resilience design approaches for improved ecosystem restoration.
- Land restoration activities engaged 1738 community members (435 female) and resulted in the rehabilitation of 33 hectares of degraded land. This included making different earth structures, such as dams, gabion structures, stabilizing catchments, contour bunds, half-moons, spillways and rehabilitating irrigation canals. Communities also undertook rangeland rehabilitation, soil bund construction, and tree planting through the distribution of seedlings.
- Improved household food security with perma-gardening training for 521 vulnerable households across Baidoa, Bardere, and Galkacyo. Each household established a permagarden and received diverse seeds, fruit trees, fodder crops, and essential tools to sustain production.
- A series of trade expos where held where around 500 individuals participated (50% women) as agricultural producers and small business owners. This demonstrated the contribution of female producers to local food production, while managing small enterprises.
- 100 (22 female) government extension workers were trained by the project on the perma-gardening approach. The extension workers have trained community households in the techniques. The approach of training existing government extension workers increases sustainability and ensures ownership of the methods used.
Initial outcomes:
- Extension workers and communities responded positively to the projects approaches, with many participants highlighting the relevance to local climate and land degradation challenges. Extension workers reported applying their new skills beyond the project activities, which indicated a strong potential for replication and ownership.
- Hands-on training combined with staff presence in the field was highly effective, creating visible shifts in participant motivation and practical understanding. However, uneven baseline skills and occasional overconfidence in replication efforts revealed the need for ongoing mentoring, technical oversight, and support systems from the project.
- Somalia has overall institutional fragility with continuous risks of lack of funding for salaries for government staff, which decreases sustainability. This also limits scalability and ability to transfer project activities to government. In addition to government extension workers, BRCiS also engages in partnerships with local actors who can help overcome these constraints and build pathways to long-term resilience and implementation of the techniques.
- The design of the project to include both rural and urban locations simultaneously within a nature-based solutions approach (rather than siloed investments) has also demonstrated potential to influence other projects and the Somali government. Lessons will be documented and knowledge products shared through online platforms and through working and coordination groups to encourage learning and replication for other stakeholders, including local authorities.
